interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: Hierarchical Experimentalist Agents
papers.authors: Abhranil Chandra , Sankaran Vaidyanathan , Utsav Dhanuka , Varun Gandhi , Scott Niekum
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to take actions in the real world and support human decision-making, yet most agents rely on parametric knowledge, fixed post-training data, retrieval, or search. This paradigm breaks down in novel domains and for sophisticated queries that cannot be answered from prior knowledge alone. Knowing the laws of physics, for instance, does not by itself enable LLMs to answer queries or complete long-horizon tasks in a complex physical system. To address this, we introduce Hierarchical Experimentalist Agents (HExA), an in-context self-improvement framework to learn from active experimentation. HExA iteratively designs and refines query-relevant experiments, learns a reusable library of composable skills from experience, and integrates experimental evidence to answer queries or take actions. HExA is training-free, compatible with any black-box model, and does not require external supervision, oracles, or offline data. To evaluate active experimentation, we introduce Interphyre, a tool-calling benchmark built on the PHYRE 2D procedural physics environment, where agents propose interventions and test hypotheses through simulation APIs. Experiments show that current LLM agents struggle in these settings, especially on the hardest levels of Interphyre. Claude Sonnet 4.6 achieves only 2% success, while HExA improves the same model to up to 77% success. HExA also improves open-weight models and outperforms agentic baselines such as ReAct and Reflexion. Moreover, using only skills learned from easier levels and transferred without active experimentation, HExA achieves 44% success, demonstrating the reusability and generalization of its learned skills. Overall, HExA shows that learning through active experimentation can help agents discover useful knowledge, acquire reusable skills, and make efficient progress on novel long-horizon tasks.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly proposes an LLM agent framework for active experimentation and skill learning, which is highly relevant to automated scientific discovery.
papers.Short digest: This paper introduces Hierarchical Experimentalist Agents (HExA), an in-context self-improvement framework that enables LLM agents to learn from active experimentation in novel domains. HExA iteratively designs experiments, learns reusable skills, and integrates evidence to answer queries, all without training or external supervision. For astronomy, this could automate the process of testing hypotheses about astronomical phenomena, such as designing observations to distinguish between AGN and starburst models. A concrete workflow could be using HExA to propose and test galaxy formation scenarios by querying simulation APIs or observational databases. The main caveat is that HExA is evaluated on a 2D physics benchmark (PHYRE), not on real astronomical data or simulations, so its performance on complex astrophysical workflows is unknown.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the paper provides any analysis of how HExA handles noisy or incomplete feedback, as astronomical data often has high uncertainty
Look for details on the skill library structure and whether skills can be composed for multi-step astrophysical workflows
Examine the computational cost of the iterative experimentation loop, as astronomical simulations can be expensive

papers.title: DEEPMED Search: An Open-Source Agentic Platform for Medical Deep Research with Introspective Verification
papers.authors: Maolin Liu , Fanyu Xu , Ruoqing Xu , Jiahang Zhang , Hao Wang , Rui Wang
papers.abstract: Navigating the deluge of heterogeneous medical data, from academic literature (PubMed) to clinical guidelines (Web) and private knowledge bases, remains a critical bottleneck for evidence-based medicine. While commercial black-box tools lack transparency, standard open-source RAG implementations frequently suffer from reasoning drift when handling complex, long-tail queries. We present DEEPMED Search, a fully open-source, agentic platform designed for transparent medical deep research. Built on a high-performance this http URL architecture, DEEPMED Search features a source-adaptive router that autonomously dispatches sub-queries to PubMed, web search, or local graph-based knowledge bases based on information density. Crucially, the platform integrates an introspective verification module, powered by a causal-consistent multi-agent debate framework, to validate retrieved evidence against diagnostic logic before synthesis. To demonstrate its robustness, we showcase DEEPMED Search's ability to autonomously decompose high-difficulty rare disease queries, filter out confounding noise, and generate structured, citation-backed research reports in minutes. By open-sourcing this software, we provide the community with a robust infrastructure to democratize access to trustworthy, glass-box medical reasoning in research and prototyping settings.
papers.Reasons for match: The paper presents an open-source agentic platform for deep research with introspective verification, which directly transfers to automated scientific discovery workflows in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: 1. The paper aims to solve the problem of navigating heterogeneous data sources (literature, web, private databases) for evidence-based research, a common bottleneck in astronomy. 2. It introduces DEEPMED Search, an open-source agentic platform that uses a source-adaptive router to dispatch sub-queries to different databases and an introspective verification module (causal-consistent multi-agent debate) to validate retrieved evidence before synthesis. 3. This matters for astronomy because it provides a transparent, glass-box framework for automated literature review and data synthesis, which could be adapted for tasks like cross-matching catalogs, extracting physical parameters from papers, or building knowledge bases for high-redshift galaxy studies. 4. A concrete workflow would be using DEEPMED Search to autonomously gather and synthesize all JWST NIRSpec spectroscopy results for little red dots at z>6, filtering out confounding noise and generating a structured, citation-backed report. 5. A key caveat is that the platform is designed for medical data (PubMed, clinical guidelines) and would require adaptation to astronomical databases (ADS, arXiv, MAST), and the introspective verification module's effectiveness on astronomical reasoning (e.g., SED fitting logic) is untested.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the architecture of the source-adaptive router and whether it can be extended to astronomical databases like ADS or arXiv.
Look for details on the introspective verification module: how the multi-agent debate is structured and whether the causal consistency checks are domain-agnostic or medical-specific.
Evaluate the open-source codebase for modularity and ease of adapting the tool set (e.g., replacing PubMed search with ADS search).

papers.title: RADIANT-PET: Reasoning-Augmented PET/CT Lesion Segmentation with Large Language Models and Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Jiasheng Wang , Tanun Jitwatcharakomol , Piyawadee Jongpradubgiat , Simeng Zhu
papers.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
papers.abstract: Accurate lesion segmentation in PET/CT is critical for oncology, yet remains challenging because physiologic tracer uptake and artifacts can mimic malignant signal. We present RADIANT-PET, a reasoning-augmented framework that couples a high-sensitivity voxel-level segmentation model with lesion-level large language model (LLM) adjudication. Candidate uptake regions are generated with a deliberately permissive segmentation stage, then converted into structured textual descriptions that summarize uptake intensity, morphology, and regional and global anatomical context. An LLM classifies each candidate as true lesion vs. false positive, optionally leveraging the radiology report as additional clinical context. To strengthen lesion-level reasoning, we further optimize a local LLM via reinforcement learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization, rewarding correct lesion classification and anatomically concordant site assignment. Across AutoPET and an OSU test cohort, RADIANT-PET consistently outperforms strong image-only baselines, with the largest improvements observed when radiology reports are provided. Overall, these results demonstrate that LLM-based lesion-level reasoning adds a novel reasoning layer beyond conventional segmentation, suppressing physiologic false positives and aligning voxel-level predictions with clinical interpretation. The project repository is available at: this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: Directly combines segmentation with LLM reasoning for medical imaging, which is highly transferable to astronomical source detection and classification (e.g., AGN vs. artifacts in JWST).
papers.Short digest: The paper asks how to reduce false positives in PET/CT lesion segmentation by adding an LLM reasoning layer. It first generates candidate uptake regions with a permissive segmentation model, then converts them into structured text descriptions of intensity, morphology, and anatomy, and uses an LLM to classify each as true lesion or false positive. For astronomy, this could be applied to JWST source detection: a permissive segmentation finds all candidate sources (including artifacts and noise peaks), then an LLM reasons about morphology, color, and context to flag true high-redshift galaxies or AGN. A concrete workflow would be running Source Extractor on a JWST image, converting each detection into a text description, and using an LLM to filter out diffraction spikes and hot pixels. A key caveat is that the method relies on structured text descriptions of candidate regions, which requires a well-defined mapping from image features to text; the paper also uses radiology reports as additional context, which has no direct analog in astronomy.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for the exact format of the structured textual descriptions: what features (intensity, morphology, context) are included and how they are extracted from the segmentation output.

Check whether the LLM is used zero-shot or fine-tuned, and whether the reinforcement learning step (GRPO) is essential or could be omitted for a new domain. Also check if the method requires a radiology report or can work with only image-derived text.

papers.title: Multimodal Graph RAG for Long-range Visually Rich Document Understanding
papers.subjects: Information Retrieval (cs.IR) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are widely applied to visual document understanding. However, comprehending long documents remains an issue by the limited context window. Though recent multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (MMRAG) can address this challenge by retrieving relevant pages. It still struggles with the visual question answering (VQA) requiring holistic comprehension of a document. To cope with this, knowledge graph (KG) that summarizes global knowledge of a document can provide an effective solution. However, most existing LLM-based KG construction methods handle only the language modality, leaving the automatic creation of multimodal KGs (MMKGs) for visually rich documents largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce a multimodal graph-based RAG approach to tackle this problem. Existing LLM-based KG methods evaluate the QA performance relying on indirect evidence such as comprehensiveness, diversity, empowerment, and so on. The lack of annotated datasets for comprehensive document-level VQA poses a significant challenge to effective model evaluation. To overcome this limitation, we also introduce a new benchmark, DLVQA (document-level VQA), which provides reference summaries and corresponding supporting facts for global document-level questions. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms existing MMRAG or KG-based approaches on multi-hop QA/VQA benchmarks and DLVQA.
papers.Reasons for match: The paper introduces a multimodal graph-based RAG approach for long document understanding, which directly maps to retrieval-augmented generation and multimodal models (LMMs) that could be adapted for astronomy literature or multi-modal data (images+text+spectra).
papers.Short digest: The paper addresses the problem of multimodal large language models struggling to comprehend long documents due to limited context windows. It proposes a multimodal graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach that builds a knowledge graph summarizing global document knowledge, enabling holistic question answering. This matters for astronomy because similar RAG+graph methods could retrieve and synthesize information across many JWST papers, instrument manuals, or multi-wavelength catalogs. An astronomer could imagine using this to build a literature agent that answers questions about high-redshift galaxy properties by retrieving and reasoning over many papers. However, the method is demonstrated on document-level VQA benchmarks, not scientific data, so the key caveat is whether the graph construction and retrieval pipeline transfers to domain-specific astronomical texts and figures.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the knowledge graph construction handles figures, tables, and captions (multimodal integration) or only text.
Look for evaluation metrics that measure factual accuracy or retrieval precision, not just QA accuracy on the new benchmark.
Assess whether the approach requires a pre-defined ontology or can build graphs from unstructured text automatically.

papers.title: ExACT: Exemplar-Driven Calibrated Refinement for Training-Free Visual Grounding in Remote Sensing Images
papers.authors: Zixiao Zhang , Lingling Li , Pei He , Xu Liu , Licheng Jiao
papers.abstract: Remote sensing visual grounding (RSVG) aims to locate specific objects in high-resolution RS imagery using free-form natural language descriptions. While recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show great potential for such open-vocabulary RSVG, their training-free adaptation is hindered by the modality gap between abstract linguistic semantics and fine-grained visual cues. In cluttered RS scenes, this gap inevitably causes severe localization drift. To bridge this gap, we propose Exemplar-driven Calibrated Refinement (ExACT), a novel training-free framework driven by a one-shot visual prompting mechanism to explicitly provide discriminative structural guidance for precise pixel-level localization. Specifically, we propose a Vision Exemplar-based Calibrator (VEC) that extracts fine-grained visual correspondences from the given exemplar to rectify the rough cross-modal priors from frozen MLLMs, effectively suppressing background artifacts and accurately outlining target boundaries. Subsequently, a Structure-Aware Refiner (SAR) employs an iterative merge-and-select clustering strategy to consolidate the calibrated priors into high-quality positive and negative geometric prompts. These prompts then guide the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to achieve precise pixel-level predictions. Extensive experiments confirm the superiority of ExACT over existing training-free and weakly-supervised methods.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly relevant to visual grounding in remote sensing, which shares challenges with astronomical image analysis (e.g., object detection in cluttered scenes).
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles visual grounding in remote sensing images, where the goal is to locate objects described by natural language. The main idea is a training-free framework called ExACT that uses a one-shot visual prompt (an exemplar image) to calibrate cross-modal priors from frozen multimodal LLMs and then refines them with a structure-aware clustering strategy to guide SAM for pixel-level segmentation. For astronomy, this could be adapted to locate specific galaxies or features in JWST images based on textual descriptions, such as 'find the little red dot with a bright core'. A concrete workflow might involve using an exemplar image of a known target to guide detection of similar objects in large survey data. However, the method is designed for remote sensing and may need adaptation to astronomical image characteristics (e.g., different noise, resolution, and object scales).
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method can handle astronomical image formats and object scales (e.g., galaxies vs. buildings).
Look for any discussion of generalizability to other domains beyond remote sensing, such as medical or astronomical imaging.

papers.title: Covering the Unseen: Information Demand Coverage Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Bingxue Zhang , Jianying Jia , Feida Zhu
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically treats context selection as ranking chunks against a single query embedding. This assumption breaks down for complex queries, such as multi-hop or ambiguous questions, where top-k selection tends to over-cover one semantic aspect while ignoring critical sub-questions. We propose GeoRAG, which recasts context selection as Information Demand Coverage Optimization. GeoRAG builds a multi-dimensional demand distribution through diverse sub-query generation and reverse-validation weighting, then selects context by minimizing the Sinkhorn-Wasserstein distance between this demand distribution and the coverage of the selected set. The resulting demand-weighted facility-location objective is monotone submodular, giving a $1-1/e$ greedy guarantee, which we approximate with a Sinkhorn-based marginal-gain surrogate. The method is unsupervised, training-free, and retrieval-agnostic. We further show that single-point, query-proximity scorers cannot cover multi-modal demands, exposing a structural limit of ranking-based selection. On six open-domain QA benchmarks, GeoRAG improves exact match (EM) by +6.5 to +7.5 points over top-k truncation (up to +9.7 on HotpotQA and ASQA) and outperforms strong baselines including MMR, DPP, BGE-Reranker, SMART-RAG, and AdaGReS, with stable gains across context budgets and sub-query generators.
papers.Reasons for match: Proposes a novel RAG method for complex queries that could directly improve literature review and data analysis in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper introduces GeoRAG, which recasts context selection in retrieval-augmented generation as an information demand coverage optimization problem. Instead of ranking chunks against a single query, GeoRAG builds a multi-dimensional demand distribution via diverse sub-query generation and selects context by minimizing the Sinkhorn-Wasserstein distance to coverage. For astronomy, this could dramatically improve RAG systems for complex multi-hop questions like 'What are the spectral properties of little red dots at z>7?' by ensuring all sub-aspects are covered. A concrete workflow would be using GeoRAG to retrieve relevant papers, spectra, and catalogs for a literature review on high-redshift AGN. The main caveat is that GeoRAG is evaluated on open-domain QA benchmarks, not on scientific or astronomical datasets, so its performance on domain-specific retrieval needs verification.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the sub-query generation method can be adapted to produce astronomy-relevant sub-questions (e.g., redshift range, wavelength coverage, object type)
Look for analysis of computational overhead, as generating multiple sub-queries and computing Sinkhorn distances may be expensive for large corpora
Examine whether the method handles multi-modal retrieval (images, spectra, tables) or only text

papers.title: Reliability, Faithfulness, and the Limits of Post-hoc Explanations of Opaque Scientific Models
papers.abstract: Post-hoc explanation methods are routinely used to interpret scientific machine learning models, with the deliverable understood to be insight into the phenomenon the model has been trained on. The transition may be taken to be secured once the model is reliable enough and the explanation faithful enough. We argue it is not. Reliability checks that the model's predictions match the phenomenon's outcomes, and faithfulness checks that the explanation matches the model, but neither checks whether the model works as the phenomenon works, which is what a claim about structure requires. The chain can support candidate hypotheses under external corroboration, but it cannot, on its own, support claims about how the phenomenon is in fact structured.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly critiques the use of post-hoc explanations (e.g., SHAP, LIME) for interpreting scientific ML models, arguing they cannot reveal true causal structure. This is highly relevant for astronomers using ML to infer physics from JWST data.
papers.Short digest: This paper asks whether post-hoc explanation methods (like SHAP or LIME) can reliably reveal the true structure of a scientific phenomenon when applied to a trained ML model. The authors argue that even if a model is accurate (reliable) and the explanation faithfully reflects the model, the explanation does not necessarily tell you how the phenomenon actually works—it only tells you what the model learned, which may be spurious correlations. For astronomy, this is a critical warning: if you train a model to predict galaxy redshift from images and then use SHAP to say 'the model uses disk color,' you cannot conclude that disk color physically causes redshift. The paper suggests that such explanations can only generate candidate hypotheses that need external corroboration (e.g., from physical simulations or controlled experiments). Before investing time in this paper, check whether it provides concrete guidelines for when post-hoc explanations are valid or offers alternative validation strategies (e.g., intervention or perturbation tests) that you could apply to your own astronomical ML workflow.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for concrete examples or case studies (e.g., from physics or biology) that illustrate the failure mode of post-hoc explanations.
Check whether the paper proposes any positive alternative (e.g., causal inference, intervention, or simulation-based validation) for astronomers to adopt.
Examine the discussion of 'external corroboration'—does it specify what kind of independent evidence is sufficient to validate a structural claim?

papers.title: Diagnosing and Repairing Factual Errors in RAG under Budget Constraints
papers.authors: Soroush Hashemifar , Havva Alizadeh Noughabi , Fattane Zarrinkalam , Ali Dehghantanha
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the factuality of large language models by grounding responses in external evidence, yet real-world deployments remain fragile. Failures often stem from missing or weakly relevant evidence, as well as from generation that does not faithfully reflect the retrieved context. Many existing approaches rely on fine-tuning, privileged access to internal model signals, or resource-insensitive escalation strategies, which limits their practicality in black-box and budget-constrained settings. We propose D2R-RAG (Diagnose-to-Repair RAG), a model-agnostic and resource-aware framework that combines lightweight failure diagnosis with adaptive repair. D2R-RAG derives interpretable failure signatures from observable signals in the query, retrieved evidence, and generated response, and then selects from a small set of corrective actions under explicit latency and VRAM constraints. Experiments on FEVER and HotpotQA show that D2R-RAG improves reliability over recent baselines and achieves better accuracy--efficiency trade-offs across multiple compute budgets. The code is available at this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses RAG reliability, a core technique for grounding LLMs in external evidence, which is key for literature review and data analysis in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles the problem of factual errors in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, especially when deployed under budget constraints like limited compute or latency. The authors propose D2R-RAG, a lightweight framework that diagnoses failures by analyzing the query, retrieved evidence, and generated response, then selects a corrective action (e.g., re-retrieval, rewriting) without needing access to internal model weights. For an astronomer, this is directly relevant because RAG is a natural way to ground an LLM in astronomical catalogs, papers, or instrument documentation. You could imagine using D2R-RAG to build a reliable assistant that answers questions about JWST data reduction or galaxy classification, where incorrect answers are costly. A key caveat is that the method is demonstrated on general-domain QA datasets (FEVER, HotpotQA), so its performance on specialized astronomical text and tables remains to be tested.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the failure diagnosis rules (e.g., missing evidence, weak relevance) are interpretable and could be adapted to domain-specific retrieval corpora.
Look for the specific corrective actions (e.g., re-retrieval, query rewriting) and whether they are compatible with astronomy-specific retrieval pipelines.
Examine the accuracy-efficiency trade-off plots to see if the method maintains high accuracy at the low compute budgets typical for individual researchers.
